evidence.field: evolution; early graph records and source interpretation
evidence.text: The 兒 evolution page lists an oracle-bone example (合集20592), a bronze example (集成06479), Chu manuscript forms, and a small-seal form. It calls the original meaning ‘infant’ and interprets the graph as highlighting the unclosed fontanel. The record labels forms and catalog numbers, but gives no dated semantic context for the oracle-bone example; the glyph sequence was not visually inspected here.
evidence.title: 漢字「兒」：字形演變

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: Shuowen textual forms; graphic analysis; readings and dated-by-source examples
evidence.text: The entry preserves a textual difference: the Great Xu Shuowen text says 从几, while Duan’s edition says 从儿; both give the ‘young child’ gloss and fontanel explanation. Its regular-script note says the upper part is written like 臼 and associates it with the fontanel, with 儿 below. It gives ér for child-related senses and ní for a surname equivalent to 倪. Its examples include 呼兒 in a Han-attributed poem, parental address and self-reference, young-man use, insult, and suffix use. These establish examples in cited texts, not first dates or a complete semantic chronology.
evidence.title: [A00277] 兒 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.text: The dossier’s inspected CUHK account reports competing interpretations of the upper part of 兒: the unclosed fontanel explanation associated with Shuowen, or paired hair buns. This leaves the exact depicted feature unresolved; neither interpretation should be stated as visually proven.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：兒

evidence.field: file description, provenance, rights, and version history
evidence.text: The exact file page identifies 兒-seal.svg as a modern vector depicting 兒 in Shuowen seal-script style and links it to Sinica source record 27.5152. It reports CC0 1.0 and public-domain terms. The current file is dated 25 November 2017; its original upload comment identifies ACC source S06201. The linked Sinica image URL returned 401, and the original SVG link could not be fetched by the web tool because it does not support SVG content. Page metadata verifies the file identity and claimed rights, but a pixel-level inspection was not possible in this research interface. Its modern redraw could illustrate a received seal form, but cannot resolve the disputed ancient referent.

evidence.text: Search surfaced a Sinica page for 儿 that describes it as the Shuowen ‘old-text and unusual graph’ for 人 and as the simplified character of 兒. This supports keeping the independent 人-shaped radical history distinct from modern simplified 儿 used for the child word.
evidence.title: 漢字「儿」：基本資料

evidence.source: Chinese Text Project, Kangxi radical entry
evidence.field: 兒 versus 儿 radical; current readings
evidence.text: The radical entry treats 儿 as the independent Kangxi radical 10, separately links 兒 as its traditional character, and reports Mandarin ér for the modern child/simplified use. It lists no origin relationship that would make this independent person-shaped radical a phonetic element in the infant graph.
evidence.title: 儿 (radical) - Chinese Text Project

evidence.field: 兒 components and person-shaped radical distinction
evidence.text: Wenlin analyzes seal-form 兒 as containing 臼 and a lower 儿 variant, but its displayed reading of the graph’s components is an editorial decomposition, not independent proof that either part was a phonetic component. It separately identifies 儿 as radical 10 and notes its use for simplified 兒.
evidence.title: Zi:兒 - Wenlin Dictionaries

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese reconstruction table
evidence.text: The table row for 兒 gives modern Pinyin ér, Middle Chinese ASCII transcription nye, and Baxter–Sagart 2014 Old Chinese *ŋe, glossed ‘child’. The supplied local row in sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv agrees: 兒 / ér / nye / *ŋe. These are readings of the whole character/word and do not establish a phonetic role for either graphic part.
evidence.title: BaxterSagartOCbyGSR2014-09-20

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese reconstruction table
evidence.text: The table row for 臼 gives modern Pinyin jiù, Middle Chinese gjuwX, Baxter–Sagart 2014 Old Chinese *C.[g]ʷəʔ, gloss ‘mortar’. The supplied local row in sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv agrees. These readings do not show that the upper part of 兒 was historically named or pronounced 臼; 臼 is a graphic comparison used in later accounts, while the ancient referent remains disputed.

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The cited Han anonymous poem has 呼兒烹鯉魚, an address to a child or household dependent; the dictionary attributes it to a Han period but does not make this a securely dated contemporary witness. Other cited examples include Tang parental address, later self-reference and young-man use, and later suffix examples. The accessible evidence does not date the first spoken child-word attestation or establish the paths from child to son, address, young person, insult, or suffix.

evidence.text: The Shuowen entry glosses 兒 as 孺子 (‘young child’). The Great Xu and Duan editions differ between 从几 and 从儿 but both explain the shape as depicting a child whose fontanel is not yet closed. This records the historical dictionary’s account, not independent confirmation of the image interpretation.

gaps: The direct Commons pages for local leads Shuowen Seal Radical 311.svg and ACC-s06201.svg failed to open; no existence, provenance, image identity, or reuse terms were verified for those exact files.

The exact 兒-seal.svg page verifies the asserted modern Shuowen-style rendering and CC0/public-domain terms, but the SVG itself could not be fetched by the web tool and the linked Sinica glyph page returned 401. Pixel-level image identity inspection therefore remains incomplete; the file is not proposed as a verified displayed glyph.

Accessible sources agree that 兒 means ‘young child’ and provide early graph catalog references, but do not date semantic context for the earliest graph record or securely date the earliest spoken child-word use.
The exact upper graphic referent remains unresolved between the fontanel interpretation and the reported paired-hair-buns interpretation. No pictorial detail should be asserted as certain.
Dictionary examples record son, address/self-reference, young-person, insulting, and suffix uses but do not establish their relative dates or semantic links.

The exact official Unicode Unihan character URLs for 儿, 兒, and 臼 were attempted but inaccessible through the web tool. Their supplied local rows are reported as local dataset evidence without claiming external verification.

The Baxter–Sagart readings are character/word readings, not evidence that 臼 was pronounced as the upper feature in ancient 兒. The character-specific account and data do not independently recover the depicted object’s name or pronunciation.
